meta_description: The Sunderland Buttonball, the Arnold Arboretum's collected trees and the first dawn redwoods back from fossil. {trees} trees across {places} places.
intro: Massachusetts has fewer giants than the West and more paperwork, which makes its old trees unusually easy to date. Harvard's Arnold Arboretum has catalogued its collection since 1872, so a paperbark maple can be traced to one wild seedling dug in China in 1907 and a white oak was core-sampled to the early 1800s. The seed that put the dawn redwood back into the ground after millions of years as a fossil arrived in Boston in 1948, and the trees grown from it still stand in the arboretum. In Cambridge, a copper beech became the city's only living Historic Landmark to stop a building going up. Out in the Connecticut River valley, the Sunderland Buttonball, a sycamore, is older than the Constitution its plaque measures it against.
